blocks.text: Producing quicklime (calcium oxide) from limestone (calcium carbonate) is one of the oldest and most basic industrial processes. Quicklime is vital in construction (cement, mortar), agriculture (soil treatment), metallurgy and many chemical industries. Limestone is an abundant sedimentary rock made mainly of calcium carbonate.

blocks.alt: A tall kiln filled with lumps: crushed limestone (CaCO3) is fed in at the top, hot gases from burning coal and natural gas enter low on the side, carbon dioxide leaves at the top and quicklime (CaO) comes out at the bottom. A box gives the reversible reaction at 900-1000 C.
blocks.caption: A lime kiln (original diagram after Figure 17.5).
blocks.long_description: Quicklime is made by heating limestone (calcium carbonate) in a lime kiln to about 900-1000 C, a thermal decomposition called calcination: CaCO3(s) <=> CaO(s) + CO2(g). In a modern kiln the charge is heated by circulating hot gases. The reaction is reversible in a closed container, so carbon dioxide is removed continuously; this shifts the equilibrium to the right and gives a large amount of quicklime.

blocks.text: Limestone is heated in a lime kiln to about 900-1000 C, a thermal decomposition called calcination: CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g) on heating. In modern kilns the charge is heated by circulating hot gases. The reaction is reversible in a closed container, so carbon dioxide is removed continuously; this shifts the equilibrium to the right and gives a large amount of product.

blocks.prompt: Why is carbon dioxide removed continuously from a lime kiln?
blocks.explanation: Removing a product shifts the equilibrium CaCO3 <=> CaO + CO2 to the right, so more limestone decomposes and more quicklime is obtained.

items: Removing CO2 drives the reaction to the right.
